opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that when we started, the three of us had been working in the field for quite a while. Guillaume and Timothée were at Meta, and I was at DeepMind, and we had all seen from the inside how these large language models were actually built. One thing that becomes clear when you do that is that you don't need thousands of people to train a very good model. You need a small, very focused team that knows what it's doing, that has good intuitions about the data, the training recipes, and how to use compute efficiently. The amount of capital is important, of course, but it's not the only factor. Efficiency matters a lot.

We also felt there was a real gap in the market. The field had become increasingly closed. Companies that had once published openly had stopped sharing, and the technology was concentrating in a few players, mostly in the US. We thought that was the wrong direction, both for the science and for the industry. We believed in open-weight models, in giving developers and enterprises something they could actually own, customize, deploy on their own infrastructure, and specialize to their use cases. That was a strong differentiator, and we didn't think the incumbents were going to take that position.

And then there was a European dimension. There was no strong European player at the frontier, and there's a lot of talent in Europe, especially in Paris, with a very good pool of researchers coming out of the schools here. So we saw an opportunity to build a company that could attract that talent, move very fast, and show that you could produce competitive models with a fraction of the resources. Our first model, Mistral 7B, came out just a few months after we started, and it was better than much larger models at the time. That was, in a way, the proof that the bet made sense.

r001.rationale: The response says the founders’ experience showed that a small team could build competitive models efficiently, but it does not clearly compare the resources they used with the resources available at their previous employers.

r002.rationale: The response describes the field becoming more closed and companies stopping open publication, but does not clearly identify unexpected changes at the founders’ own previous employers as a motivation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that we didn't see it as crazy at the time, even if a lot of people did. When Guillaume, Timothée and I started talking about it in early 2023, we had all been building large language models inside big labs, at DeepMind and at Meta. So we knew what it actually took to train a frontier model. And the honest answer is that it took far fewer people than the headcount of those organizations suggested. The core work was done by maybe a dozen or two dozen people who really understood the data pipelines, the training stack, the infrastructure. The rest was overhead, and sometimes the overhead slowed you down.

So the question was really, do you need ten thousand people to do this, or do you need twenty very good people, enough compute, and the freedom to move quickly? We believed it was the second. And we believed the big companies had a structural problem, which is that they had decided to close everything. GPT-4 came with a paper that had no technical details. That was a signal to us that the field was moving toward secrecy, and we thought that was both bad for the ecosystem and an opening for someone who was willing to be open.

The other piece is that we were in Europe. There was a lot of talent here, trained in places like École Polytechnique, ENS, working in Paris and London, and there was no company that gave them a real alternative to going to the Bay Area. We thought there was an opportunity to concentrate that talent, and to build something that enterprises, and particularly European enterprises, would actually want, which is a model they could run themselves, modify, and deploy without sending their data to an API they don't control.

And then there's a bit of a bet on the science. The scaling laws work, Chinchilla had shown you could be much more efficient about how you spent compute, and we were convinced that smaller, well-trained models could compete with much bigger ones. Mistral 7B was the proof of that. It wasn't about matching the biggest lab on raw size, it was about being much more efficient per dollar and per parameter, and giving that to people openly. That's the kind of thing that's hard to do from inside a large company, and quite natural to do from a small one.

r001.rationale: The response says their experience building language models at DeepMind and Meta showed them that frontier models could be trained by a small, expert team with enough compute, rather than the much larger headcount of established labs.

r002.rationale: It describes major labs moving toward secrecy as an opportunity, but does not clearly identify an unexpected change in the direction of the founders’ own previous employers as a motivation.

astra-6.text:
We felt that the technology was still very young, and that a small team with the right expertise could make a meaningful contribution. Training these models requires compute, of course, but it also depends on a lot of scientific and engineering choices. Having more resources doesn’t mean you’ve exhausted the possibilities for doing things more efficiently.

There was also an opportunity to build a different kind of company around this technology: one that made models more accessible and gave developers more control over how they used and deployed them. So the ambition wasn’t simply to reproduce what the established labs were doing. It was to build strong models with a small, focused team and offer a different way of putting them into people’s hands.

r001.rationale: It says a small team with the right expertise could contribute and that efficiency choices matter, but does not clearly state that the founders’ machine-learning expertise let them build good models with fewer resources than their previous employers had.

r002.rationale: It describes a desire to build a different kind of company, but does not identify unexpected changes in the founders’ previous employers as a motivation.

sol-6.1.text:
When we started Mistral, we felt there was still a lot of room to improve how these models were built. The field was moving very quickly, and having a very large team or a lot of compute didn’t necessarily mean you would find the next good idea first. A small team with strong experience could move fast and make meaningful progress.

We also saw an opportunity to build a company around open models, giving developers and enterprises more control over how they use the technology. So the ambition wasn’t simply to reproduce what the established companies were doing. It was to make capable models more accessible and adaptable, and we thought there was room for an independent company to do that.

r001.rationale: It says an experienced small team could move quickly, but does not clearly state that the founders’ machine-learning expertise let them build good models with fewer resources than their former employers had.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention unexpected changes in the direction of the founders’ previous employers.
